description: Learning cards with subtitle, body paragraphs, and takeaway per card.

cards.title: The Most Important Product You've Never Seen
cards.subtitle: Your car stopped working because a factory in Taiwan flooded.
body: You've never heard of TSMC, but your $60,000 vehicle is a paperweight because their fab went offline.
Invisible infrastructure only becomes visible when it breaks.
cards.takeaway: Semiconductors are the hidden foundation of modern life.

cards.title: Geography Is Destiny in Silicon
cards.subtitle: One earthquake in Taiwan and your iPhone production stops.
body: 90% of advanced chips come from one island—on a fault line, 100 miles from China.
You optimized for efficiency and got fragility.
cards.takeaway: Concentration creates vulnerability at civilizational scale.

cards.title: One Machine Controls the Future
cards.subtitle: One company in the Netherlands decides who builds advanced chips.
body: ASML makes the only machine that can print cutting-edge semiconductors. $150M each. No alternatives.
The chokepoint isn't the factory—it's the machine inside.
cards.takeaway: Control the tools and you control the output.

cards.title: Fabrication Is the New Oil
cards.subtitle: The U.S. invented semiconductors. Then outsourced manufacturing.
body: Intel, Apple, Nvidia designed the chips. But Taiwan makes them.
The CHIPS Act is $52B worth of realizing you gave away strategic infrastructure.
cards.takeaway: Manufacturing capability is strategic power.

cards.title: The Design-Manufacturing Split
cards.subtitle: Apple designs the chip. TSMC decides if it gets made.
body:
• $2B chip design complete
• Now you're on a waitlist
• Competitors in the same line
TSMC became the chokepoint nobody planned for.
cards.takeaway: Separating design from manufacturing created new dependencies.

cards.title: Moore's Law Was Never a Law
cards.subtitle: Your roadmap assumes chips double every two years. They won't.
body: The industry spent fifty years organizing around Moore's observation. Now physics is hitting walls.
Moore's Law was coordination dressed up as inevitability.
cards.takeaway: Self-fulfilling prophecies work until the physics says no.

cards.title: Military Demand Built the Industry
cards.subtitle: Nobody wanted your $1,000 chip. Except the Pentagon.
body: Early chips were expensive and worthless to consumers. But missiles needed small computers.
Silicon Valley's origin story starts at the Department of Defense, not in a garage.
cards.takeaway: Government funding absorbed the risk private capital wouldn't touch.

cards.title: The Foundry Model Rewrote Power
cards.subtitle: You don't need a fab anymore. You need TSMC's permission.
body: Before TSMC, you needed a billion-dollar fab. After, design talent alone could build a chip company.
They democratized design and concentrated power in manufacturing.
cards.takeaway: Lowering barriers in one place can raise them in another.

cards.title: You Can't Stockpile Innovation
cards.subtitle: You hoarded a million chips. Last year's chips. Already obsolete.
body: Strategic reserves work for oil. Not for semiconductors.
The real advantage is access to the next fabrication node, not a warehouse of old ones.
cards.takeaway: In technology, inventory buys time but not capability.

cards.title: Export Controls Are Weapons
cards.subtitle: China built a $100B chip industry. The U.S. ended it with a memo.
body: No missiles. Just export restrictions. China's foundries went from cutting-edge to stranded overnight.
Export controls target the toolchain, not the product.
cards.takeaway: Controlling critical supply chains is a form of power projection.

cards.title: Taiwan: Two Fault Lines
cards.subtitle: An earthquake or an invasion. Either stops chip production.
body: TSMC's fabs sit on a seismic fault line AND 100 miles from China.
Taiwan's 'silicon shield' theory: the world needs their chips too much to let it fall.
cards.takeaway: Deterrence based on economic necessity is still a gamble.

cards.title: Talent Is the Real Bottleneck
cards.subtitle: You built a $20B fab. Now you need 3,000 engineers who don't exist.
body: Subsidies got you the building. Now you need decades of expertise you can't buy.
The building is the easy part. The people are the bottleneck.
cards.takeaway: Money can buy facilities but not institutional knowledge.

cards.title: Copying Chips Is Harder Than It Looks
cards.subtitle: The Soviets stole chip designs for thirty years. Still couldn't build them.
body: The design is 10% of the problem. Manufacturing knowledge is embedded in people and years of trial and error.
You can steal the recipe and still not make the dish.
cards.takeaway: Tacit expertise can't be photographed or stolen.

cards.title: The Supply Chain Has No Backup
cards.subtitle: A chemical plant in Japan catches fire. Global chip production stops.
body:
• Materials from Japan
• Gases from Europe
• Equipment from Netherlands
• Fabrication in Taiwan
One supplier down = entire chain breaks. Optimized for cost, not resilience.
cards.takeaway: Specialization creates efficiency and eliminates every backup.

cards.title: Speed Wins, Scale Follows
cards.subtitle: You hit 3nm six months after TSMC. Apple already signed with them.
body: First to the next node gets Apple, Nvidia, and the Pentagon.
You're not racing other fabs. You're racing irrelevance.
cards.takeaway: In semiconductors, being first compounds into dominance.

cards.title: Software Ate the World, Chips Ate Software
cards.subtitle: Your AI startup raised $100M. Then Nvidia said no GPUs until Q4.
body: Every software revolution has a hardware dependency. AI needs GPUs. Cloud needs server chips.
Software gets the headlines. Chips do the work.
cards.takeaway: The silicon layer decides what's possible.

cards.title: Government Money Doesn't Guarantee Results
cards.subtitle: China spent $100B on chip independence. Half the fabs are abandoned.
body: Subsidies bought buildings. They didn't buy talent or institutional knowledge.
Industrial policy works when it amplifies existing strengths, not conjuring from nothing.
cards.takeaway: Money is necessary but not sufficient for building ecosystems.

cards.title: The Company That Makes the Machines Rules
cards.subtitle: You own a $10B fab. ASML owns you.
body: ASML doesn't make chips—they make the machines that make chips.
You can't print cutting-edge semiconductors without them. No alternatives exist.
cards.takeaway: The bottleneck isn't the factory—it's the machine inside it.

cards.title: Consumer Demand Funds Military Power
cards.subtitle: You bought an iPhone. You funded the chip in a cruise missile.
body: Consumer electronics fund semiconductor R&D. That tech goes into smartphones and fighter jets.
The Pentagon depends on a commercial market it doesn't control.
cards.takeaway: High volume drives down costs and funds the next node.

cards.title: The Next War May Be Won in a Cleanroom
cards.subtitle: Your missiles can't hit the target. Their chips are two generations ahead.
body: Precision guidance, drone swarms, electronic warfare—all run on semiconductors.
The side with better chips has weapons the other side can't build.
cards.takeaway: The cleanroom is now a strategic military asset.
